evals.prompt: Review this Go handler: func ParseReservation(body []byte) Reservation { var r Reservation; if err := json.Unmarshal(body, &r); err != nil { panic(err) }; return r }. This function parses the raw HTTP request body from a client. Is panicking here appropriate?
evals.expected_output: Flags panicking on malformed request input as wrong since it's an external/expected failure, not a broken invariant, and recommends returning an error instead.

assertions.text: Flags panic on external/user input as inappropriate

evals.prompt: Review this Go code: if err != nil && strings.Contains(err.Error(), "not found") { return handleMissing() }. Is this a robust way to detect a not-found condition? What would you recommend instead?
evals.expected_output: Flags string-matching on error text as fragile since it breaks when message wording changes, and recommends errors.Is or errors.As against a defined sentinel or typed error.

assertions.text: Flags string matching on Error() as fragile

evals.prompt: In our Go inventory service, we have a function LoadHotelConfig(id int) that reads a config file bundled at compile time using a package-level var compiled with regexp.MustCompile on a hardcoded pattern string. Separately, a function ParseGuestEmail(input string) validates an email address supplied by a guest during checkout. Which of these two should use panic vs return an error, and why?
evals.expected_output: Explains that regexp.MustCompile on a hardcoded, compile-time-constant pattern is fine to panic on since failure only indicates a programmer bug in that code, while ParseGuestEmail must return an error since guest input is external and expected to sometimes be invalid.

assertions.text: Approves panic-style MustCompile for compile-time-constant pattern as a programmer-error case
Requires ParseGuestEmail to return an error since it handles external input
